result.note: Tested the Supreme Court's July 2026 order, the RAF's role, and the absence of a law on police facial recognition; skipped political concessions and party claims.

questions.prompt: In July 2026, the Supreme Court heard petitions alleging excess force against student protesters at Jantar Mantar. Consider the following statements about its order:
items: It ordered the release of every protester under the age of 18.
It barred coercive action against demonstrators.
It required police to preserve recordings from drones, body cameras and closed-circuit television.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explain: All three were part of the order. Chief Justice Surya Kant also told authorities to hold protesters' personal data without publishing it.
questions.source: India's Supreme Court has ordered every under-18 protester released, barring coercive action against demonstrators and requiring police to preserve all footage of the crackdown.

questions.prompt: In July 2026, an internal inquiry found that which federal anti-riot unit deployed at Jantar Mantar had issued pellet guns to its personnel?
questions.explain: The Rapid Action Force issued pellet guns to at least a dozen personnel on 20 July and stopped using them on 23 July. Delhi Police denied issuing them, and the RAF sits under separate central command.
questions.source: The Rapid Action Force (RAF), the federal anti-riot unit deployed at Jantar Mantar, issued pellet guns to at least a dozen personnel on the morning of July 20, according to an internal inquiry.

questions.prompt: Consider the following statements about police surveillance of protesters in India as of July 2026:
items: A petition seeking to have the surveillance declared unconstitutional and the data destroyed is before the Delhi High Court.
India has a law specifically governing police use of facial recognition technology.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explain: Student activist Aishe Ghosh moved the Delhi High Court, but India currently has no law governing police use of facial recognition. Demonstrators had photographed a police van, branded Ikshana, fitted with 360-degree cameras.
questions.source: India currently has no law governing police use of facial recognition.
